---
title: "Week 3: Mapping What We See and What We Fear"
---

## Theme: The Built Environment: Street-Level Data and Perceived Safety

Does a neighborhood feel safe? And does that feeling match reality?
Street-level imagery and computer vision tools allow us to quantify the
perceived environment --- but also raise profound questions about
surveillance, privacy, and whose fear gets measured. This week we map
the built environment using OpenStreetMap and introduce heat map
visualization of perception data.

## Classroom Lab Demonstration

**Legal Focus:** Privacy law and the Fourth Amendment in public space;
legal implications of using street-level imagery for government public
health surveillance; informed consent and passive data collection.

**Health Focus:** How the physical characteristics of neighborhood
environments (lighting, vacancy, greenspace) shape perceived safety and
mental health through environmental stress pathways.

**Data:** OpenStreetMap via the osmdata R package (openstreetmap.org);
SafeGraph foot traffic data (safegraph.com --- provided via Carmen for
academic use); vacancy rate data from ACS via tidycensus.

**R Code:** osmdata::opq() and osmdata::add_osm_feature() to query OSM;
sf::st_as_sf() to convert to spatial object; ggplot2 geom_sf() for dot
maps and heat maps; biscale package for bivariate choropleth mapping of
two variables simultaneously.

- Query OpenStreetMap for Columbus street network and building
  footprints using osmdata R package

- Load ACS vacancy rate data at census tract level via tidycensus;
  compute vacancy quartiles

- Produce a bivariate choropleth map of streetlight density vs. vacancy
  rates using the biscale package in R

- Identify 3 spatial outliers where perceived safety (perception score)
  diverges from infrastructure data (vacancy, lighting)
